issues.legal_issue: A disciplinary finding is not a finding based on no evidence merely because the complainant is not examined at the regular enquiry.
material_facts: The complainant did not testify at the regular enquiry despite attempts to secure his attendance.
Two officers who conducted the preliminary enquiry testified about that enquiry and the complainant’s recorded statement.
The Patwari and other bank employees testified, including evidence identifying a letter as written and signed by the employee.
issues.conclusion: The complainant’s absence did not make the enquiry a case of no evidence; the High Court’s additional ground for invalidating the disciplinary decision was unsustainable.
issues.legal_principle: The finding must be assessed against the evidence actually presented in the disciplinary enquiry. Here, testimony about the preliminary enquiry and the recorded statement, together with testimony from other witnesses and evidence identifying the letter, provided evidence on which the enquiry officer could rely. The Court referred to the established distinction between a finding unsupported by evidence and a finding reached on evidence whose weight or sufficiency is challenged.

rule.if: disciplinary_enquiry and complainant_not_examined and (preliminary_enquiry_witnesses_testified or other_relevant_evidence_presented)

predicates.disciplinary_enquiry: An employer conducted a disciplinary enquiry into alleged employee misconduct.
predicates.complainant_not_examined: The person who made the complaint did not testify at the regular disciplinary enquiry.
predicates.preliminary_enquiry_witnesses_testified: People who conducted an earlier investigation testified at the disciplinary enquiry about that investigation and material gathered in it.
predicates.other_relevant_evidence_presented: Other witnesses or documentary evidence relevant to the alleged misconduct were presented at the disciplinary enquiry.

issues.definition: When a complainant does not testify in a disciplinary enquiry, testimony from preliminary investigators or other relevant evidence can mean that the finding still has evidentiary support.

issues.legal_issue: A procedural defect in a disciplinary enquiry does not automatically invalidate the enquiry or punishment when the employee nevertheless receives a fair hearing and the defect causes no demonstrated prejudice.
material_facts: The governing service regulation required copies of earlier witness statements to be supplied at least three days before examination of witnesses; it separately gave the employee a right to inspect and take notes of listed documents.

Copies of the witness statements and other listed materials were not supplied, but the employee was allowed to inspect them and take notes more than three days before the relevant witnesses testified.
The complainant whose statement was not supplied did not testify at the regular enquiry; the Patwari whose statement was not supplied did testify.
The employee did not object during the enquiry that the absence of copies impaired cross-examination or his defence.
The lower appellate court asserted prejudice but did not identify a specific way in which the employee’s defence had been impaired.
issues.conclusion: The documents did not have to be supplied as copies under the regulation, and although the witness statements were not supplied as required, the employee had substantial access to them and no prejudice was established. The enquiry was fair, the punishment was not invalidated, and the suit challenging it was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: For a disciplinary enquiry, a breach of a substantive requirement must ordinarily be treated differently from a breach of a procedural requirement. A procedural breach generally calls for examination of whether the employee was prejudiced and, considering the circumstances as a whole, received a fair hearing; substantial compliance may suffice. A breach falling within the categories of no notice, no opportunity, or no hearing, or a breach of a procedural requirement fundamental in nature, may not be assessed in the same way. For a mandatory procedural requirement designed for the employee’s benefit, waiver may also be relevant. The Court relied on Regulation 68(b)(i) and (iii) of the State Bank of Patiala (Officers’) Service Regulations, 1979; sections 99 of the Code of Civil Procedure and 465 of the Code of Criminal Procedure as illustrations of the approach to procedural error; and Ridge v. Baldwin, Vasudevan Pillai v. City Council of Singapore, Calvin v. Carr, Janakinath Sarangi v. State of Orissa, K.L. Tripathi v. State Bank of India, Managing Director, ECIL v. B. Karunakar, Dhirendra Nath Gorai v. Sudhir Chandra Ghosh, and Krishan Lal v. State of Jammu and Kashmir.

rule.if: disciplinary_enquiry and procedural_copy_requirement_applied and required_copies_not_supplied and materials_reviewed_before_relevant_testimony and employee_did_not_claim_defence_impairment_during_enquiry and no_specific_defence_impairment_identified

predicates.disciplinary_enquiry: An employer conducted a disciplinary enquiry into alleged employee misconduct.
predicates.procedural_copy_requirement_applied: The procedure governing the enquiry required copies of earlier witness statements to be provided to the employee before witness examination.
predicates.required_copies_not_supplied: The employer did not provide the required copies of the earlier witness statements to the employee.
predicates.materials_reviewed_before_relevant_testi: The employee was allowed to inspect the relevant materials and take notes before the witnesses testified.
predicates.employee_did_not_claim_defence_impairmen: The employee did not tell the enquiry that the absence of copies impaired the ability to cross-examine witnesses or present a defence.
predicates.no_specific_defence_impairment_identifie: The courts reviewing the enquiry did not identify a specific way in which the employee’s defence was impaired.

issues.definition: When required copies are not supplied in a disciplinary enquiry, but the employee reviews the materials before testimony, raises no claim of impaired defence during the enquiry, and no specific impairment is identified, the procedural breach does not invalidate the punishment.
